broad.question: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: High-entropy induced a glass-to-glass transition in a metallic glass.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper establishes that high‑entropy effects can substantially alter the atomic energy landscape in metallic glasses (PMC9023469::web::017). This hypothesis builds on that by using a minor compositional tweak (Hf addition) to further manipulate the free energy landscape through enhanced mixing enthalpy and atomic size mismatch.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This approach introduces Hf as a dopant in phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloys, capitalizing on its intrinsic properties to further hinder crystallization—a strategy distinct from the bonding motifs proposed in other dopant scenarios and not addressed in the original study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount (1–3 at.%) of hafnium (Hf) into a phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy will improve its glass‑forming ability and thermal stability by leveraging Hf’s strong negative mixing enthalpy and substantial atomic size to further disrupt crystallization.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An amorphous phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced by conventional arc melting and rapid quenching, characterized by high configurational disorder and a metallic bonding network.
hypothesis.intervention: Add 1–3 at.% hafnium to the alloy’s composition prior to melting, ensuring thorough mixing and homogeneity during arc melting and subsequent rapid solidification.
hypothesis.conditions: The Hf content should remain within 1–3 at.% so as to avoid phase separation or the formation of Hf‑rich intermetallic compounds; processing must be done under inert atmosphere with sufficient remelting steps to guarantee uniform distribution.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Hafnium, with its large atomic radius and a strong negative heat of mixing with transition metals, introduces local chemical heterogeneity and enhances atomic size mismatch, thus increasing the overall excess configurational entropy.
hypothesis.mechanism: The presence of Hf in the alloy disrupts regular atomic packing by inducing local compositional fluctuations. Its strong chemical affinity with other metallic constituents and sizable atomic size elevate the free energy barrier for crystallization. This thermodynamic penalty for nucleation helps to extend the stability of the amorphous state by suppressing crystallization kinetics.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: DSC analysis should show an extended supercooled liquid region and an upward shift in the crystallization onset temperature relative to the baseline alloy. XRD and TEM should confirm the retention of an entirely amorphous structure, and mechanical testing (e.g., nanoindentation) may reveal enhanced hardness or modulus due to a more stabilized short-range order.
hypothesis.baseline: The phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy fabricated without the addition of Hf under identical processing conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: If the Hf concentration is too high (above ~3 at.%), there is a risk of Hf segregation or the formation of Hf‑rich intermetallic phases which would negate the glass‑forming benefits.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Although Hf’s role in increasing mixing entropy and disrupts crystallization is supported by general metallic glass principles, the precise magnitude of the effect in phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloys remains to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of alloy samples: one batch with 1–3 at.% Hf added and a control batch without Hf. Use consistent arc melting and rapid quenching protocols along with multiple remelting cycles to ensure compositional homogeneity.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to record changes in the supercooled liquid region and the onset temperature of crystallization.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the amorphous structure and rule out the presence of Hf‑rich phases.
Nanoindentation or dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) to compare any enhancements in mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf‑doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in glass‑forming ability (e.g., no extension of the supercooled liquid region or shift in crystallization onset) or if phase segregation is observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: High-entropy induced a glass-to-glass transition in a metallic glass.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper demonstrates that high‐entropy enhances the energetic and structural disorder in metallic glasses (PMC9023469::web::017). This hypothesis extends that concept by further destabilizing crystallization through increased atomic size mismatch.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a specific compositional intervention (minor Y doping) that leverages entropic and size-mismatch effects, as opposed to introducing localized directional bonds, to improve glass-forming ability and thermal stability in a metallic system.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (1–2 at.%) of a large-atomic-radius dopant such as yttrium (Y) to a phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy will improve its glass‑forming ability and thermal stability by increasing atomic size mismatch and packing frustration without relying on directional bonding.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A fully amorphous phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced by conventional arc melting and rapid melt spinning, characterized by high configurational entropy and a disordered metallic bonding environment.
hypothesis.intervention: Incorporate 1–2 at.% yttrium into the precursor mix prior to melting, ensuring complete dissolution and homogeneous distribution.
hypothesis.conditions: The Y content must be maintained in the 1–2 at.% range to avoid forming Y‑rich intermetallic phases; processing requires careful control of melting and cooling conditions under an inert atmosphere.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Y atoms, due to their significantly larger atomic radius compared to the other constituent elements, create local atomic size mismatches that increase packing frustration and hinder the nucleation of crystalline phases.
hypothesis.mechanism: Unlike localized covalent bonding, in metallic glasses the dominant bonding is delocalized. The introduction of Y increases the excess configurational entropy via atomic size mismatch. This enhanced mismatch disrupts the regular packing, thereby raising the free energy barrier for crystallization, leading to an extended supercooled liquid region and improved thermal stability.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: DSC scans are expected to show a broader supercooled liquid region and a higher or more distinctly observed glass transition (Tg). XRD and TEM should confirm that the amorphous structure is maintained, while nanoindentation or DMA may reveal modest improvements in hardness or elastic modulus.
hypothesis.baseline: The phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy synthesized without any yttrium addition, under identical processing conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: If the Y content exceeds ~2 at.%, there is a risk of forming Y‑rich intermetallic compounds that could deteriorate the amorphous character; conversely, if below 1 at.%, the atomic size mismatch may be insufficient to impact nucleation kinetics.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While atomic size mismatch is a recognized mechanism for enhancing glass-forming ability, the exact quantitative improvement in the supercooled liquid region width or thermal stability is uncertain without further systematic studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one series with 1–2 at.% Y added and one series of the baseline alloy without Y. Use identical arc melting and melt-spinning procedures under inert atmosphere with multiple remelting cycles for homogeneity.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess Tg, supercooled liquid region width, and crystallization exotherms.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the continued amorphous structure and absence of Y‑rich intermetallic phases.
Nanoindentation or dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) to measure any changes in mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y‑doped samples do not show a statistically significant extension of the supercooled liquid region, an upward shift or sharpening of the glass transition, or present any detectable Y‑rich crystalline phases compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C7

source_paper.title: Decoupling between calorimetric and dynamical glass transitions in high-entropy metallic glasses.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion enhance thermal stability and retard crystallization in metallic glasses (PMC8219663)
hypotheses.what_is_new: Introducing a minor high-field-strength dopant (yttrium) to further tailor atomic-level diffusion and nanoscale chemical homogeneity in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys—a strategy not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a high-field-strength element such as yttrium (≈2 at.%) to phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys enhances their glass forming ability and thermal stability.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy in the amorphous state (for example, Pd20Pt20Cu20Ni20P20) produced by rapid quenching.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce about 2 atomic percent yttrium during alloy preparation.
hypothesis.conditions: Melt-spinning under inert atmosphere with cooling rates comparable to baseline; care must be taken to ensure that the yttrium level does not exceed the limit where phase separation or crystallization-inducing precipitates occur.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The yttrium atoms, due to their large atomic size and high field strength, induce additional local strain fields and enhance chemical disorder by increasing atomic size mismatch, which refines the nanoscale chemical heterogeneity.
hypothesis.mechanism: The enhanced size mismatch and local bonding effects further hinder atomic mobility by increasing the activation energy for long-range diffusion (i.e. delaying the formation and percolation of shear transformation zones). This further depresses the α-relaxation dynamics and retards crystallization, leading to improved thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Y-doped alloy should exhibit a higher crystallization activation energy, increased viscosity near Tg, and an improved critical casting thickness due to enhanced glass forming ability.
hypothesis.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys processed without yttrium addition.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only for low yttrium contents (typically 1–3 at.%) beyond which excessive doping may lead to undesirable phase separation or crystallization.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement (e.g., percentage increase in crystallization activation energy) is uncertain, though a moderate improvement (<20%) is expected based on similar diffusion-suppressing effects observed in high-entropy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of the baseline phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy and one set with 2 at.% Y added. Subject both sets to identical rapid quenching (e.g., melt spinning) and characterize them using DSC (to determine Tg and Tx), DMA (to assess α-relaxation behavior), and TMA (to measure viscosity near Tg).
measurements: DSC curves and determination of onset Tg and Tx
Activation energies from Kissinger analysis
DMA loss modulus and α-relaxation temperatures
Viscosity measurements near Tg via TMA
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy shows no significant improvement (within experimental error) in glass forming ability or thermal stability (e.g., similar Tg, Tx, and activation energies compared to the baseline), the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order in metallic alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s insights on how athermal events can alter SRO (PMC12508472::web::010) and the general concept that external dynamic perturbations can interfere with equilibrium atomic self-organization.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a single intervention using controlled acoustic vibrations during solidification—after precise simulation-based calibration—to actively steer the formation of a disordered SRO, thereby enhancing glass-forming ability and thermal stability, an approach not addressed in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Continuous application of low-amplitude, high-frequency acoustic vibrations during rapid solidification can perturb atomic self-organization at the solid–liquid interface, leading to a more disordered SRO and thereby improving the glass‐forming ability and thermal stability of phosphorus‐containing high-entropy alloys.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A molten phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy prepared for rapid quenching.
hypothesis.intervention: Integrate an in situ acoustic vibration system that applies controlled, low-amplitude ultrasound (or high-frequency acoustic waves) during the quenching process, where the optimal frequency and amplitude are pre-determined by simulation to ensure atomic-scale perturbations without inducing cavitation or unwanted nucleation.
hypothesis.conditions: The acoustic parameters (frequency, amplitude, and duration) must be calibrated through detailed simulation studies and sensitivity analyses such that the energy input remains within the linear response regime of the material, affecting only localized regions at the advancing solid–liquid interface during the entire rapid solidification window.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An acoustically perturbed SRO state featuring enhanced chemical disorder at the interface, which reduces the formation of nucleation-favorable atomic clusters and increases the barrier to crystallization.
hypothesis.mechanism: The applied acoustic vibrations serve as an external athermal mixing mechanism analogous to the athermal events described in the paper, which disrupt the inherent self-organizing tendencies of atoms at the solid–liquid interface. This results in a frozen SRO configuration that is more disordered, thereby enhancing the kinetic barrier against crystallization. Simulation-based calibration ensures that the vibrations are strong enough to perturb atomic order without causing adverse effects like cavitation or accelerating diffusion.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples processed with acoustic vibrations during quenching are expected to show (i) broader and more diffuse XRD scattering profiles, (ii) an elevated crystallization onset temperature in DSC measurements, and (iii) local SRO metrics indicating increased disorder compared to samples quenched without acoustic intervention.
hypothesis.baseline: Identical alloy samples rapidly solidified without the application of acoustic vibrations.
hypothesis.boundary: If the vibration amplitude or frequency falls outside the calibrated optimal range, the intervention may either be too weak to affect SRO or too strong, triggering unwanted nucleation events or cavitation effects. Its success is contingent upon maintaining finely tuned vibrational parameters.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise vibrational parameters (frequency and amplitude) that yield the desired modification in SRO without adverse effects remain to be accurately determined via comprehensive simulation and preliminary experimental studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one processed with the calibrated acoustic vibrations during rapid quenching and one without. Analyze both groups using XRD to evaluate amorphous scattering profiles, DSC to measure crystallization onset temperatures, and local structural probes (e.g., pair distribution function analysis or atom probe tomography) to quantify SRO.
measurements: XRD profiles for amorphous vs. crystalline features
DSC crystallization onset temperature
Local SRO characterization metrics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vibrated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in terms of increased amorphous stability or alterations in local SRO relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Designing High Entropy Bulk Metallic Glass (HE-BMG) by Similar Element Substitution/Addition.

hypotheses.builds_on: The concept from the paper that increasing atomic size disparity (as captured by the δ′ parameter) can be achieved via similar element substitution to control the amorphous phase.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This approach tests the introduction of a rare-earth element (cerium) to modulate lattice distortion in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys—a strategy that extends the principles outlined in the paper to a different class of dopants and alloy systems.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount of cerium (approximately 1–3 at.%) into phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will improve glass-forming ability and thermal stability by increasing the overall atomic size disparity and lattice distortion.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys with a balanced mix of refractory and transition metals making up a moderate range of atomic sizes.
hypothesis.intervention: Substitute 1–3 at.% of one of the larger metallic components with cerium, ensuring homogeneous distribution in the melt.
hypothesis.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective under rapid solidification conditions where cerium can uniformly participate in the alloy matrix; if cerium segregates or if cooling rates are too slow, the benefits may not be realized.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An increased atomic size mismatch that raises the δ′ parameter, leading to enhanced lattice distortion and a more deeply metastable amorphous structure.
hypothesis.mechanism: Cerium has a comparatively large atomic radius relative to typical transition metals in such alloys. Its substitution increases atomic size disparity, which in turn elevates the lattice distortion, hindering the mobility necessary for crystallization during cooling. This increases both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: An observable widening of the supercooled liquid region along with an increase in the maximum critical casting diameter compared to alloys without cerium, indicating improved resistance to crystallization.
hypothesis.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys without cerium addition that demonstrate comparatively lower values of δ′ and more readily crystallize.
hypothesis.boundary: The effectiveness is limited to low cerium concentrations; high levels might provoke phase separation or induce deleterious intermetallic compounds due to solubility limits.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the expected mechanistic benefits are supported by principles of atomic size mismatch, the quantitative improvement in glass stability remains to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples with 0%, 1%, and 3% cerium substitution under identical casting conditions. Use DSC to measure the supercooled liquid region and determine the critical casting diameter via XRD structural analysis.
measurements: DSC curves to assess Tg, Tx, and ΔT
Critical casting diameter measurements
XRD analysis to confirm amorphous structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cerium-containing samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the supercooled liquid region or critical casting thickness compared to the no-cerium baseline, or if they exhibit signs of enhanced crystallinity, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the novel use of an ultrafast laser flash treatment post electrodeposition as a processing intervention to further kinetically trap the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys—a strategy not addressed in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A single post‐deposition ultrafast laser flash treatment applied to phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys can induce transient localized melting and rapid quenching that further suppresses nucleation and enhances the stability of the amorphous state.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An as‐deposited, amorphous phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy produced by nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition.
hypothesis.intervention: Immediately after electrodeposition, subject the alloy film to a controlled, ultrafast laser pulse (in the nanosecond to microsecond range) with energy calibrated to induce surface melting of a thin layer without causing significant elemental segregation.
hypothesis.conditions: The laser fluence must be precisely set so that only a superficial re‐melt occurs and subsequent quenching is rapid enough to avoid crystallization; the treatment should be compatible with the substrate and not induce thermal damage.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The laser pulse generates localized, transient melt‐zones that, upon rapid quenching, eliminate incipient nucleation sites and reinforce the amorphous structure by effectively “resetting” the atomic configuration.
hypothesis.mechanism: By providing a brief, high‐temperature pulse followed by ultra‐rapid cooling, any minute crystalline seeds that may have begun forming during deposition are eradicated. This additional quenching step increases the effective cooling rate beyond the intrinsic electrodeposition rate, leading to a more deeply frozen disordered state with enhanced thermal stability.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The laser‐treated samples should demonstrate a higher crystallization onset temperature and exhibit a more homogenous amorphous structure (as determined by TEM/SAED and DSC), compared to untreated controls.
hypothesis.baseline: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys produced by nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition and left without any post‐treatment.
hypothesis.boundary: The effective outcome is contingent on tuning the laser energy; if the energy is too low the intervention is ineffective, whereas excessive energy could provoke local crystallization or damage the film.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise improvement (e.g., in degrees Celsius increase in crystallization temperature) depends on optimizing the laser parameters, and the optimal window for treatment energy is uncertain without preliminary calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Divide as‐deposited phosphorus‐containing alloy films into two groups. Subject one group to the specified ultrafast laser pulse treatment while leaving the other as a control. Use DSC to measure crystallization and glass transition temperatures and employ TEM/SAED to analyze the microstructure. Compare the thermal stability and amorphous quality between the two groups.
measurements: DSC to determine the crystallization onset and glass transition temperatures
TEM/SAED to assess amorphous versus crystalline structure
Surface morphology analysis (e.g., AFM) to check for laser‐induced damage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser‐treated samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature or if they exhibit evidence of crystallization/damage compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypothesis.boundary: This intervention should succeed when the annealing temperature is optimally chosen to allow relaxation without triggering crystallization. Too long or too high an annealing temperature could promote unwanted crystallization, and too short a treatment might be ineffective.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal annealing time and temperature window needs careful calibration; the quantitative improvement in thermal stability is sensitive to these parameters and may vary with slight deviations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 samples. Immediately subject one set to sub–Tg annealing (e.g., T_g - 20 K for 10 minutes) while keeping the other set as-quenched. Perform DSC analysis on both sets under identical reheating conditions.
measurements: DSC to determine differences in T_g, T_x, and exothermic peak areas.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sub–Tg annealed samples do not show a statistically significant extension of the supercooled liquid region, delay in crystallization onset, or improvement in the amorphous fraction relative to the as-quenched ones, the hypothesis is falsified.
